results.name: Bomba de la Barceloneta
results.why_it_is_special: La Cova Fumada (open since 1944) claims to have invented the bomba — a deep-fried garlicky potato ball stuffed with ground beef, served with spicy sauce. Still priced at around €2.20, it's a working-class classic in a no-frills, cash-only bar packed with locals. Arrive by 11 am to avoid long waits.

results.name: Pa amb Tomàquet
results.why_it_is_special: Bread rubbed with ripe tomato, drizzled with olive oil and salt — the most elemental Catalan dish. Bodega Can Ros (Carrer de Roger de Flor 303, metro Joanic) is a small neighbourhood bar that makes one of the best versions in the city.

results.name: Esqueixada de Bacallà
results.why_it_is_special: A refreshing shredded salt-cod salad with tomatoes, onions, and olives — a Catalan summer staple. Polleria Fontana (Carrer de Sant Lluís 9, metro Joanic) is an informal, welcoming tapas spot in the heart of Gràcia.

results.name: Fideuà
results.why_it_is_special: Fideuà is the Catalan noodle-based alternative to paella, cooked with short pasta and seafood. Restaurant Canet (Carrer Canet 38, metro Sarrià) is a quaint family restaurant in a quiet corner of the Sarrià neighbourhood, serving one of Barcelona's best versions.

results.name: Calçots amb Romesco
results.why_it_is_special: Calçots are flame-grilled sweet onions dipped in romesco or salvitxada sauce — a seasonal Catalan ritual (roughly November–March). Can Cargol is one of the best places in Barcelona proper to enjoy them in season.

results.name: Botifarra amb Mongetes
results.why_it_is_special: Traditional Catalan pork sausage served with white beans — hearty, simple, and deeply local. Bar La Plata is a tiny, legendary bar with only four tapas on its menu, and botifarra is one of them. Its stripped-back approach is a hallmark of authentic Barcelona dining.

results.name: Crema Catalana
results.why_it_is_special: Catalonia's answer to crème brûlée — a custard flavoured with cinnamon and lemon zest, with a caramelised sugar crust. Granja Dulcinea, a historic granja (milk bar) on Carrer de Petritxol, is a beloved local institution for this dessert.

results.name: Vermouth hour
results.why_it_is_special: The hora del vermut (vermouth hour) is a deeply Catalan pre-lunch ritual. Els Sortidors del Parlament, a beautiful old bar on Carrer del Parlament, specialises in vermouth and local wine alongside an extensive tapas menu — an ideal starting point for a vermouth crawl in the trendy Sant Antoni neighbourhood.

results.name: Escalivada
results.why_it_is_special: Smoky grilled vegetables (aubergine, peppers, onions) — the name comes from the Catalan escalivar ("to cook in ashes"). Can Culleretes, founded in 1786 and one of Barcelona's oldest restaurants, serves classic Catalan dishes including escalivada, cannelloni, and Catalan-style piglet.

results.name: Suquet de Peix & classic Catalan menu
results.why_it_is_special: Suquet is a traditional Catalan fisherman's stew of fish and potatoes. 7 Portes, open since 1836 at Port Vell Marina, is a grand Catalan institution serving suquet, daily-changing paellas, and regional classics in a historic dining room.
